questions.title: Chained Append Operations with Heterogeneous Types
questions.question: Demonstrate the fluent API of `StringBuilder` by chaining multiple `.append()` calls using a `String`, an `int`, a `char`, and a `double` to construct a single formatted string[cite: 21, 22].
questions.explanation: `StringBuilder` manages an internal mutable array of characters that expands dynamically as characters are added[cite: 18, 21]. Unlike `String`, where concatenation allocates a new object on every step, `StringBuilder.append()` modifies the existing buffer in place and returns `this`—the reference to the active buffer instance[cite: 6, 9, 18, 21]. This enables fluent method chaining across different data types (`append(String)`, `append(int)`, `append(char)`, `append(double)`)[cite: 21]. Each append operation converts the argument into characters and writes them directly into the backing array without synchronization overhead, delivering fast text assembly in single-threaded contexts[cite: 21].
hints: Instantiate a `StringBuilder` using `new StringBuilder("Score: ");`[cite: 21].
Chain mutator methods together in a single statement: `sb.append(...).append(...);`[cite: 21].
Convert the completed buffer to a string using `.toString()` before printing[cite: 1, 21].

questions.title: Positional Insertion at Index Zero
questions.question: Prepend a prefix string at index 0 of an existing `StringBuilder` instance using `.insert()` and display the modified contents[cite: 21, 22].
questions.explanation: The `StringBuilder.insert(int offset, String str)` method inserts a character sequence at a specified index in the buffer[cite: 21]. When inserting at index 0, existing characters are shifted to the right by the length of the inserted string using native memory copying (`System.arraycopy`)[cite: 9, 15, 21]. If the insertion causes the total character count to exceed the buffer's capacity, the backing array expands automatically[cite: 21]. Inserting at index 0 allows prepending text dynamically without allocating a separate temporary buffer[cite: 21].
hints: Create an initial buffer: `StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("World");`[cite: 21].
Call `.insert(0, "Hello ")` to shift existing characters and insert text at the front[cite: 21].
Verify the resulting string starts with the prepended prefix[cite: 20, 21].

questions.title: In-Place StringBuilder Character Reversal
questions.question: Reverse the character sequence of a `StringBuilder` in place using `.reverse()` and print the reversed result[cite: 21, 22].
questions.explanation: The `.reverse()` method of `StringBuilder` reverses the sequence of characters in place within the backing buffer[cite: 21]. It operates using a two-pointer approach, swapping characters from outer boundaries inward until the pointers meet in the middle[cite: 5, 9, 19]. The algorithm correctly handles surrogate pairs (such as emojis or supplementary Unicode characters) so that multi-byte code units are not corrupted during swapping[cite: 21]. Because the mutation happens in place on the internal array, no new buffer or intermediate `String` object is allocated[cite: 18, 21].
hints: Initialize the buffer with your target string: `new StringBuilder("Java");`[cite: 21].
Invoke `.reverse()` directly on the instance[cite: 21].
Observe that the original buffer object is mutated directly without reassignment[cite: 18, 21].

questions.title: Range Deletion and Specific Character Removal
questions.question: Remove a range of characters from a `StringBuilder` using `.delete(start, end)` and remove a single character at an exact index using `.deleteCharAt()`[cite: 21, 22].
questions.explanation: `StringBuilder` provides two methods for character deletion: `.delete(int start, int end)` and `.deleteCharAt(int index)`[cite: 21]. The range deletion method removes characters within the half-open interval `[start, end)` (inclusive of `start`, exclusive of `end`)[cite: 20, 21]. Subsequent characters are shifted left to fill the gap using `System.arraycopy`, and the length is updated accordingly[cite: 9, 15, 21]. Similarly, `deleteCharAt(index)` removes the character at a specific zero-based index and shifts remaining characters left by one position[cite: 21]. Both operations modify the buffer in place with zero heap allocations[cite: 18, 21].
hints: Remember that `.delete(start, end)` excludes the character at index `end`[cite: 20, 21].
Use `.deleteCharAt(index)` to remove a single character at a specific position[cite: 21].
Ensure indices fall within valid bounds `[0, sb.length()]` to avoid `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`[cite: 18, 21].

Original: Java 21 Framework
After range delete: Java Framework
After deleteCharAt: Java Framewor

questions.title: Character Inspection and Substring Search in Buffer
questions.question: Locate the index of a target substring inside a `StringBuilder` using `.indexOf()` and retrieve specific characters using `.charAt()`[cite: 22].
questions.explanation: Like the `String` class, `StringBuilder` implements `CharSequence`, providing search and inspection methods like `.indexOf()` and `.charAt()`[cite: 18, 20, 21]. Calling `.indexOf("target")` scans the backing character array forward and returns the starting index of the first occurrence, or `-1` if not found[cite: 9, 20]. Calling `.charAt(index)` retrieves the character at that specific zero-based index in $O(1)$ time[cite: 18]. This allows developers to locate tokens and inspect characters directly inside mutable buffers without converting them to immutable `String` instances first[cite: 18, 21].
hints: Find the starting position of a word using `int idx = sb.indexOf("Target");`[cite: 20].
Inspect a character at a specific index using `char c = sb.charAt(idx);`[cite: 18, 21].
Verify that `indexOf` returns `-1` when the searched substring is absent[cite: 9, 20].

Index of 'Backend': 5
Char at index 0: 'J'
Char at index 5: 'B'

questions.title: Delimited Sequence Construction without Trailing Separator
questions.question: Build a comma-separated list of numbers from 1 to 100 into a `StringBuilder` ensuring no trailing comma is added at the end, and display the first 20 characters and total length[cite: 22].
questions.explanation: Constructing delimited lists in a loop requires handling the boundary condition where the separator should not appear after the final element[cite: 3, 21]. Appending a delimiter after every item and calling `.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1)` at the end requires an extra deletion step[cite: 21]. A cleaner, more efficient approach checks index conditions inside the loop: if `i > 1`, prepend the comma before appending the next number[cite: 3, 21]. This builds the formatted sequence directly in the buffer without requiring cleanup passes[cite: 21].
hints: Loop from `1` through `100`[cite: 14].
Conditionally append the delimiter: `if (i > 1) sb.append(",");`[cite: 3, 21].
Append the integer value on each iteration[cite: 21].

Suffix preview: ...96,97,98,99,100
Total character length: 291

questions.title: Concatenation Performance Benchmark: Operator vs Builder
questions.question: Benchmark the performance difference between repeated string concatenation (`+=`) and `StringBuilder.append()` across 100,000 operations, logging elapsed time[cite: 2, 18, 22].
questions.explanation: Because `String` is immutable, repeated concatenation inside loops creates substantial performance and memory overhead[cite: 2, 3, 18]. In a loop of $N$ iterations, writing `str += "x"` allocates an intermediate `StringBuilder`, appends the string, and allocates a new `String` object via `toString()` on every iteration[cite: 1, 3]. This copies $1 + 2 + \dots + N$ characters, resulting in $O(N^2)$ quadratic time complexity and creating thousands of short-lived heap objects[cite: 3]. In contrast, `StringBuilder` uses a mutable backing array that expands geometrically, achieving amortized $O(1)$ append operations and $O(N)$ linear time complexity[cite: 3, 15, 21].
hints: Benchmark `StringBuilder` across 100,000 appends using `System.nanoTime()`[cite: 2, 21].
Use a smaller iteration count for `+=` (e.g., 10,000) to keep execution time reasonable[cite: 18].
Convert the elapsed nanosecond differences into milliseconds[cite: 2].
questions.expectedOutput:
100,000 appends with StringBuilder completed in: 2 ms
Performance verdict: StringBuilder provides linear O(N) performance.

questions.title: Vowel Stripping via In-Place Buffer Deletion
questions.question: Remove all English vowels (A, E, I, O, U, case-insensitive) from a string in place using `StringBuilder.deleteCharAt()`[cite: 21, 22].
questions.explanation: Filtering characters from a `StringBuilder` in place requires careful index management[cite: 21]. The loop inspects each character from index 0 to `sb.length() - 1`[cite: 14, 21]. When a vowel is detected (`"aeiouAEIOU".indexOf(c) != -1`), calling `sb.deleteCharAt(i)` shifts all subsequent characters to the left, decreasing the buffer's length by one[cite: 8, 12, 17, 21]. Because the character at index `i + 1` shifts into index `i`, the loop index must decrement (`i--`) so the newly shifted character is evaluated on the next iteration[cite: 21]. This removes matching characters in place without allocating a secondary buffer[cite: 18, 21].
hints: Traverse using `for (int i = 0; i < sb.length(); i++)`[cite: 14, 21].
Check for vowels: `"aeiouAEIOU".indexOf(sb.charAt(i)) != -1`[cite: 8, 12, 17, 21].
Call `sb.deleteCharAt(i);` and decrement `i--` to account for the leftward character shift[cite: 21].

Original:  Java Developer Community
No Vowels: Jv Dvlpr Cmmnty

questions.title: URL Space Encoding via In-Place Replace
questions.question: Implement URL space encoding (replacing spaces with `%20`) using `StringBuilder.replace()` across an input string[cite: 20, 22].
questions.explanation: URL percent-encoding replaces spaces (`' '`) with the three-character sequence `"%20"`[cite: 20, 22]. Using `StringBuilder.replace(int start, int end, String str)` performs this substitution directly in the buffer[cite: 21]. When a space is located at index `i`, `sb.replace(i, i + 1, "%20")` replaces the single space character with the 3-character string, shifting subsequent characters to the right and expanding the buffer length by 2[cite: 21]. The loop index then advances past the inserted replacement (`i += 2`) to continue scanning the remainder of the text without re-checking the newly added characters[cite: 21].
hints: Traverse the buffer with `for (int i = 0; i < sb.length(); i++)`[cite: 14, 21].
When `sb.charAt(i) == ' '`, invoke `sb.replace(i, i + 1, "%20")`[cite: 21].
Advance `i += 2` to skip past the newly inserted `%20` sequence[cite: 21].

Encoded URL: search%20java%20backend%20engineering

questions.title: Nested Numeric Triangle Builder
questions.question: Construct a 4-row numeric triangle pattern as a single multi-line string within a `StringBuilder` using nested loops, and print the completed string[cite: 14, 22].
questions.explanation: Assembling complex multi-line text grids in a single `StringBuilder` buffer avoids issuing multiple `System.out.print` I/O system calls[cite: 1, 21]. The outer loop manages rows from 1 to $N$, while the inner loop manages columns from 1 to the current row index `i`[cite: 14]. On each inner iteration, `sb.append(j)` appends the column digit[cite: 14, 21]. After the inner loop completes each row, `sb.append('\n')` appends a newline delimiter[cite: 1, 21]. The entire grid is constructed in memory and printed in a single I/O operation via `System.out.print(sb.toString())`[cite: 1, 21].
hints: Use an outer loop `for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)` for rows[cite: 14].
Use an inner loop `for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++)` to append column digits[cite: 14, 21].
Append `\n` at the end of each row inside the outer loop[cite: 1, 21].

questions.title: Arbitrary-Precision Decimal Addition via StringBuilder
questions.question: Implement arbitrary-precision addition of two large numbers represented as strings using `StringBuilder` without using `BigInteger`[cite: 21, 22].
questions.explanation: Standard 64-bit primitive types (`long`) overflow when handling numbers with more than 19 digits[cite: 5]. Adding arbitrarily large numbers requires simulating grade-school column addition using character buffers[cite: 21]. Two pointers start at the least significant digits (the right ends) of both strings and move leftward[cite: 9, 14]. On each step, the digits are converted to integers, added together with any carry from the previous column, and the resulting digit (`sum % 10`) is appended to a `StringBuilder`[cite: 14, 21]. The carry updates to `sum / 10`[cite: 7]. After the loop processes all digits and any final carry, reversing the buffer produces the final sum in $O(\max(N, M))$ time[cite: 21].
hints: Initialize pointer indices at `num1.length() - 1` and `num2.length() - 1`[cite: 8, 9].
Loop while `i >= 0 || j >= 0 || carry > 0`[cite: 14, 15].
Append `total % 10` to `sb`, update `carry = total / 10`, and call `sb.reverse()` at the end[cite: 7, 21].

questions.title: Binary String Addition Engine
questions.question: Implement a binary string addition method that adds two base-2 binary strings (`"1011" + "1101"`) and returns their binary sum using `StringBuilder`[cite: 22].
questions.explanation: Binary addition operates on base-2 columns using the binary arithmetic rules $0+0=0$, $1+0=1$, $1+1=10_2$ (sum 0, carry 1), and $1+1+1=11_2$ (sum 1, carry 1)[cite: 7]. Pointers iterate backward from the least significant bits of both strings[cite: 9, 14]. On each step, bits are converted to integers by subtracting `'0'`, added together with the carry, and the resulting bit (`sum % 2`) is appended to a `StringBuilder`[cite: 7, 14, 21]. The carry updates to `sum / 2`[cite: 7]. Reversing the buffer produces the final binary sum without relying on integer parsing, avoiding 32-bit or 64-bit overflow on long binary strings[cite: 5, 21].
hints: Iterate backward from the end of both strings: `while (i >= 0 || j >= 0 || carry > 0)`[cite: 14, 15].
Compute the sum bit using `sum % 2` and the carry using `sum / 2`[cite: 7].
Reverse the accumulated `StringBuilder` before returning the binary string[cite: 21].

questions.title: Run-Length Encoding Compression via StringBuilder
questions.question: Implement run-length string compression (e.g., `'aabcccccaaa'` becomes `'a2b1c5a3'`) using `StringBuilder` with pre-allocated capacity[cite: 18, 22].
questions.explanation: Run-length encoding (RLE) compresses contiguous repeating characters into character-count pairs[cite: 18, 20]. Pre-allocating capacity with `new StringBuilder(text.length())` ensures the buffer has sufficient space upfront, preventing array reallocations during encoding[cite: 18, 21]. The algorithm traverses the string, tracking consecutive matching characters[cite: 14, 18]. When the character at the current index differs from the previous one, the previous character and its count are appended to the buffer, and the counter resets to 1[cite: 3, 18]. After the loop completes, the final character and count are appended[cite: 3]. If the compressed string is not shorter than the original, the original string is returned instead[cite: 18].
hints: Pre-allocate capacity: `new StringBuilder(text.length())`[cite: 18, 21].
Traverse from index 1 to `length() - 1`, checking if `s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(i - 1)`[cite: 14, 18].
Return the shorter of the original or compressed string[cite: 18].

questions.title: Integer to Roman Numeral Converter via StringBuilder
questions.question: Convert an integer from 1 to 3999 into its standard Roman numeral representation using lookup arrays and a `StringBuilder` buffer[cite: 16, 22].
questions.explanation: Converting an integer to a Roman numeral uses a greedy subtraction algorithm across ordered value-symbol pairs[cite: 16]. Roman numerals follow subtractive rules where numbers like 4 ('IV') and 9 ('IX') are represented using paired symbols[cite: 16]. Two parallel arrays store standard values and their corresponding Roman symbols in descending order: 1000 ('M'), 900 ('CM'), 500 ('D'), 400 ('CD'), 100 ('C'), 90 ('XC'), 50 ('L'), 40 ('XL'), 10 ('X'), 9 ('IX'), 5 ('V'), 4 ('IV'), and 1 ('I')[cite: 16]. A `while` loop subtracts the largest matching value repeatedly, appending the corresponding symbol to a `StringBuilder` until the number reduces to zero[cite: 15, 21].
hints: Store descending numeric values and symbols in parallel arrays, including subtractive combinations like 900 ('CM') and 4 ('IV')[cite: 16].
Use a loop: `while (num >= values[i]) { sb.append(symbols[i]); num -= values[i]; }`[cite: 15, 21].
Advance to smaller denominations as the number reduces[cite: 16].

questions.title: Word-Preserving Line Wrap Engine
questions.question: Implement a text wrapping engine that wraps a long sentence at a specified line width without splitting words, using a `StringBuilder` cursor[cite: 22].
questions.explanation: Word wrapping formats text to fit within a fixed column width without breaking words across line boundaries[cite: 22]. The algorithm splits the input text into word tokens around whitespace[cite: 4, 8]. It maintains a running count of characters on the current line[cite: 8]. For each word, it checks whether adding the word and a space would exceed the target line width[cite: 8]. If it fits, the word is appended to the current line; if it would exceed the width, a newline character (`\n`) is appended, and the word starts a new line[cite: 1, 21]. This formats text into bounded lines using a single `StringBuilder` buffer[cite: 21].
hints: Split the input sentence into words: `text.split("\\s+")`[cite: 4, 8].
Track current line length in a variable: `lineLen`[cite: 8].
If `lineLen + word.length() + 1 > maxWidth`, append `\n`, reset `lineLen`, and append the word[cite: 1, 8, 21].
